s: A written constitution does four distinct jobs, and most constitutional disputes can be located by asking which job is at stake.
Articles I–III create Congress, the presidency and the federal judiciary, specify how officers are chosen, and prescribe the procedures by which each branch acts.
Bicameralism and presentment (Art. I, § 7), the Appointments Clause (Art. II, § 2) and the "case or controversy" limit (Art. III, § 2) are procedural rules, not mere formalities.
Many of the Court's separation-of-powers decisions turn on whether the prescribed procedure was followed.
Power is divided horizontally among three coequal branches, each with checks on the others, and vertically between the national government and the states.
The national government is one of enumerated powers (Art. I, § 8; Tenth Amendment).
The states retain a general "police power" to legislate for health, safety, welfare and morals.

The Bill of Rights, the Reconstruction Amendments, and the limits on states in Art. I, § 10 (no ex post facto laws, bills of attainder, or laws impairing contracts) protect individuals against the government.
Because Article V makes amendment difficult, ordinary majorities cannot change constitutional rules by statute.
That entrenchment is what makes judicial review consequential: a judicial ruling on constitutional meaning can be displaced only by amendment or by the Court itself.
